title: The impact of light and colour on psychological mood: a cross-cultural study of indoor work environments
research_question: To determine whether indoor lighting and colour would have any systematic impact on the mood of people working indoors.

participants.description: 468 females and 520 males, aged 18 to 65 years (mean 39.4 SD 9.85 years), working in indoor environments (offices, schools, industrial premises) in four countries: Argentina (27° S), Saudi Arabia (26° N), Sweden (56° N), and the UK (52° N).
participants.recruitment: Employees at a number of larger, as well as smaller, indoor work environments. Sampling criteria included male and female personnel generally working at least three-quarters of full time, during daytime. Night-shift workers and those with previous records of prolonged illness were excluded.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Real indoor work environments (offices, schools, industrial premises) in four countries (Argentina, Saudi Arabia, Sweden, UK) with varying latitudes and seasonal day lengths. Environmental features included objective illuminance, subjective lighting appraisal, subjective interior colour appraisal, and distance to nearest window.

measures.instrument: 12 four-grade rating scales (rested/tired, alert/drowsy, awake/sleepy, interested/bored, efficient/inefficient, devoted/indifferent, secure/anxious, friendly/angry, happy/sad, confident/hesitating, independent/dependent, strong/weak) combined into a total index (coefficient α = 0.82).

Four-graded scale: 1) clearly insufficient, much too dark; 2) slightly insufficient, a little bit too dark; 3) just right, neither too bright nor too dark; 4) very bright and glaring, too much light (between seasons consistency coefficient α = 0.82).

Four-graded scale: 1) no colour at all, very subdued and monotonous; 2) colours are rather neutral; 3) some colour but not very vivid; 4) very colourful and vivid (between seasons consistency coefficient α = 0.86).

measures.construct: Distance from workplace to nearest window

measures.instrument: Calibrated luxmeters, measured around noon with clear or light overcast sky, artificial illumination generally on.
Computed from sunrise to sunset for each region at five times of the year.

findings.antecedent: Country (Sweden, UK) and Season (winter vs. summer)
findings.mechanism: Seasonal variations in length of day (amount of daylight through windows) and sub-SAD.
findings.quote: there were considerable seasonal differences in Sweden... and in the UK... with positive values in summer and negative values in winter.

findings.mechanism: Countries closer to the equator have smaller seasonal differences in day length.
findings.quote: In Argentina and Saudi Arabia the seasonal differences were much smaller... these variations did not reach significance.

findings.antecedent: Objective horizontal illuminance (lux) (partitioned into 3 groups: 28-300, 301-600, 601-2150 lux)
findings.mechanism: The vast majority of subjects perceived lighting as 'just right' despite large objective variations, suggesting subjective appraisal is more critical than objective lux levels.
findings.quote: The impact of illuminance on the participants' mood was not significant at any time and there were no significant interaction effects.

findings.antecedent: Distance to nearest window (partitioned into 4 groups: 0-2m, 2.1-5m, 5.5-10m, 11-100m)
findings.mechanism: Bimodal distribution suggests beneficial effects for close proximity (0-2m) and for very far distances (>10m, effectively windowless), possibly due to adjustment to windowless environments.
findings.quote: The distance to the nearest window... had a significant impact on mood in February (August in Argentina)... distances up to 2 m from the window had the most beneficial effect on the emotions. However, being very far from a window seemed better than being 5–10 m away.

findings.antecedent: Subjective lighting conditions (much too dark, a little too dark, just right, too much light)
findings.mechanism: Mood is lowest when lighting is perceived as 'much too dark', highest when 'just right', and declines when 'too bright'. This aligns with an optimal arousal or processing fluency level.
findings.quote: The participants' emotional status was at its highest when the lightness was considered to be just right.

findings.antecedent: Subjective interior decoration / colour (no colour, neutral colour, some/much colour)
findings.mechanism: More colourful work environments contribute to a more positive mood, possibly through arousal modulation or aesthetic preference.
findings.quote: the index of emotional status was higher throughout the year for those who had the most colourful work environment.

findings.mechanism: Minor differences in mood between males and females, with males in Argentina and Saudi Arabia reporting higher well-being than females.
findings.quote: There were minor differences between males and females (F(1, 972)=6.72, p < 0.01)

findings.mechanism: Minor differences in mood between younger and older participants, with older participants in Saudi Arabia reporting higher well-being than younger ones.
findings.quote: between the younger and older participants (F(1, 972) = 6.69, p < 0.01).

findings.mechanism: Workplaces further from windows tend to have lower objective illuminance, though this correlation is modest.
findings.quote: There was a modest negative correlation between workplace illuminance and the distance to the nearest window, which varied between r= -0.18 and r= -0.27

mechanisms: Seasonal variations in day length influencing mood, particularly in higher latitudes.
Subjective appraisal of lighting conditions (too dark, just right, too bright) affecting mood, suggesting an optimal range for perceived light.
The presence and proximity of windows, and potentially the 'view function' of windows, influencing mood.
The use of colour in interior decoration contributing to a more positive psychological mood, possibly through aesthetic preference or arousal modulation.
implementation_implications: Consider seasonal impact and access/distance to windows in design.
Supplement physical lighting measurements with qualitative assessments from occupants.
Implement good colour design to contribute to a more positive mood, with moderate increases in colourfulness rather than highly saturated colours.
Treat light and colour as part of a complex system for a healthy building.

tables.description: Number of participants and dropout by country.
Distribution of distance from workplace to nearest window (n=988).
Mean and standard deviation of illuminance values (lux) at workplaces during different seasons for each country.
Mean index of emotional status for different sub-groups (gender, age) in the four countries.
Means and standard deviations of the dependent and independent variables (emotional index, illuminance, distance to window, subjective lighting, subjective colour) across five occasions.
Mean emotional status as a function of subjective lightness for each season, with F-statistics and p-values.

limitations: Comparisons in absolute figures between countries are difficult due to semantic differences in translated scales.
Objective lighting measurements (horizontal illuminance) did not show significant impact on mood, suggesting a need for other measures like luminance.
The study did not fully disentangle the 'view function' of windows from the 'daylight delivery function'.

The study focused on subjective colour appraisal, and highly saturated colours in laboratory studies sometimes showed undesirable results, suggesting caution in applying strong colours in real environments.
The study is cross-sectional in nature for some comparisons, and longitudinal studies are needed for more detailed analysis of lighting parameters.
